lines.cap: Out in space, a star can explode with the force of billions of bombs, and you would hear absolutely **nothing**.
So why does the loudest event imaginable make total silence?
It's all down to what **sound** really is: a **vibration**, passed from particle to particle.
Let's see how sound travels, what makes it high or low, loud or quiet, and how we use sounds we can't even hear.
Every sound you've ever heard began with something **vibrating**.
To **vibrate** means to move quickly **back and forth** about a fixed position. Sound is a form of **energy** made by those vibrations.
Pluck a guitar or violin **string**, and it vibrates.
Hit a **drum**, and its skin vibrates.
When you speak, your **vocal cords** vibrate: two flaps of tissue in your throat. Hum, and you can feel them buzz.
A loudspeaker's **cone** vibrates in and out, pushing on the air.
Twang a ruler over the edge of a desk, and you can see it: the end blurs as it vibrates.
Press a finger on a ringing bell, and the sound **stops**, because you've stopped the vibration.
That's strong evidence that **vibration is the source of all sound**, even when it's too small or too fast to see.
So how does a vibration reach your ear? The vibrating object knocks into the **particles** next to it.
They bump into their neighbours, which bump into theirs, passing the disturbance along. That travelling disturbance is a **sound wave**.
The material it travels through is the **medium**: a **solid**, a **liquid** or a **gas**. In a cup-and-string telephone, it's the tight string.
Watch one particle. It vibrates back and forth as the wave passes, but it **doesn't travel with the wave**. It ends up where it started.
So no air has to flow from a singer to your ear. Each particle just vibrates in place; it's the **energy** that travels.
Sound is a **longitudinal** wave: the particles vibrate in the **same direction** that the wave travels.
That makes regions where particles are squeezed together, called **compressions**, and regions where they're spread out, called **rarefactions**, moving out from the source.
It's like a line of people, shoulder to shoulder. Shove the first, and a bump passes down the line, but everyone stays put.
Try it at home: sprinkle rice on cling film stretched over a bowl, then bang a baking tray nearby. The sound makes the film vibrate, and the rice **jumps**!
Here's the secret of the silent star. Sound needs particles to pass the vibration along, so it **cannot travel through a vacuum**.
A **vacuum** is a space with **no particles** at all, like outer space.
In the **bell-jar experiment**, an electric bell hangs inside a sealed glass jar, not touching the sides. At first, you can hear it clearly.
Then a vacuum pump removes the air, and the ringing gets **quieter and quieter**...
...even though you can still **see** the hammer hitting the bell. With almost all the air gone, you can hardly hear it.
Let the air back in, and the sound returns.
So sound **needs a medium**, but **light doesn't**: you can still see the bell.
That's why space is **silent**, even though light crosses it easily. You'd hear nothing from a real explosion in space, whatever the films show!
So astronauts on a spacewalk talk by **radio**: radio waves, like light, can cross a vacuum.
Remember: **No air, no aware**. No medium, no sound.
Sound takes time to travel. In air, it moves at about **330 to 340 metres per second (m/s)**: roughly **1 kilometre every 3 seconds**.
The speed depends on the medium: the more closely the particles are packed, the faster they pass the vibration along.
So sound is **slowest in gases**, like air.
It's **faster in liquids**: about **1,500 m/s** in water, more than four times faster.
And it's **fastest in solids**: about **5,000 m/s** in steel.
So sound isn't fastest in air, as many people think: it's slowest! Remember: **Solids Speed, Gases Go slow**.
Light is far faster: about **300,000,000 m/s**, nearly a **million times** quicker than sound.
So in a thunderstorm, you see the lightning at once, but hear the thunder **seconds later**, as the sound crawls behind.
Count the seconds between the flash and the bang, and **divide by three**. That's roughly how far away the storm is, in **kilometres**.
Count to 6, and it's about **2 kilometres** away.
And 340 is only a typical value: sound is a little faster in warm air than in cold air.
Fun fact: the **crack** of a whip is a tiny sonic boom, because its tip moves faster than sound!
Sounds differ in two ways: **pitch** and **loudness**. Each depends on a different feature of the vibration.
**Pitch** is how high or low a sound seems. It depends on the **frequency**: the number of complete vibrations, or waves, each second.
Frequency is measured in **hertz (Hz)**. **1 Hz** means **one vibration per second**.
A **high frequency** gives a **high pitch**, like a whistle or a small bird.
A **low frequency** gives a **low pitch**, like a bass drum or a big dog's growl.
**Loudness** depends on the **amplitude**: the size of the vibration, from the rest position to the furthest point.
A **big amplitude** gives a **loud** sound; a **small amplitude**, a **quiet** one.
Remember: **Fast Pitch, Big Bang**. Fast vibrations give a high pitch; big vibrations give a big bang.
The two are **independent**: a sound can be high and quiet, or low and loud. A higher note is **not** automatically louder.
So to play a **higher note** on a guitar, raise the frequency: **tighten** the string, **shorten** it, or use a **thinner** one.
To play **louder**, pluck **harder**. That gives a **bigger amplitude**, but the same pitch.
We can't see sound, but we can **picture** it. A **microphone** turns the vibrations into an electrical signal.
An **oscilloscope** draws that signal on a screen as a wavy line, called a **trace**.
The **spacing** of the waves shows the **frequency**: waves packed close together mean a high pitch; waves spread out, a low pitch.
The **height** of the waves shows the **amplitude**: tall waves are **loud**; short waves are **quiet**.
Make a sound **louder**, and the waves grow **taller**. If the pitch hasn't changed, the spacing stays the same.
Make it **higher**, and **more waves** squeeze into the same width of screen. If the loudness hasn't changed, the height stays the same.
Your turn. Trace **A** has tall waves, far apart. Trace **B** has short waves, close together. Describe each sound.
Trace **A** is **loud** and **low-pitched**. Trace **B** is **quiet** and **high-pitched**.
In the exam, use the right words: **amplitude** for loudness, and **frequency**, or wave spacing, for pitch.
Your **ear** turns sound waves into signals for your brain. Let's follow a sound in.
The **pinna**, the flap you can see, funnels sound into the **ear canal**.
The wave makes the **ear drum** vibrate: a thin, tight membrane, like the skin of a drum.
Three tiny **bones** in the middle ear pass the vibrations on to the **cochlea**: a coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear.
Sensitive cells in the cochlea turn the vibrations into **nerve signals**, which travel to your **brain**.
But you can only hear a certain range of frequencies, called the **hearing range**: about **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**.
Remember the two twenties: **20 to 20k**, where k means **thousand**.
Sounds outside that range are still real sound. A dog hears a dog whistle at about **25,000 Hz**, but you hear nothing at all.
The top of your range drops as you get older, which is normal.
**Very loud sounds** carry lots of energy, and can damage the delicate cells in the cochlea, sometimes **permanently**.
So wear **ear defenders** near loud machinery, and keep your headphones turned down.
Sound can **reflect**, or bounce, off surfaces, especially hard, flat ones like a cliff or a tiled wall.
A reflected sound that you hear a moment after the original is an **echo**.
Soft materials, like curtains and carpet, **absorb** sound instead. That's why an empty room sounds echoey.
**Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency **above 20,000 Hz**: too high for humans to hear.
It reflects off boundaries inside the body, so in **medical scans**, the echoes build a picture, like a baby before it's born, with no harmful radiation.
In **cleaning**, ultrasound shaken through a liquid scrubs the dirt off jewellery and lenses.
And in **sonar**, ships and submarines send ultrasound pulses into the water and time the echoes. With a known speed, the time gives the distance.
Try one. A pulse goes straight down, and its echo returns **4 seconds** later. In water, sound travels at about **1,500 m/s**.
In 4 seconds, the sound travels 1,500 × 4 = **6,000 m**. But that's **there and back**, so cut it in half: the sea is **3,000 m** deep.
Bats and dolphins find their way using the echoes of their own high-pitched squeaks. It's called **echolocation**.
Scientists describe any wave with a few key measurements. You've met two already: **frequency** and **amplitude**.
**Wavelength** is the length of one complete wave, say from one compression to the next. It's a distance, so it's measured in **metres**.
Its symbol is the Greek letter **lambda**: **λ**.
The **time period**, **T**, is the **time** for one complete wave to pass, in **seconds**.
It's the opposite of frequency. At **5 Hz**, five waves pass each second, so each one takes **one fifth of a second**: 0.2 s.
So **T = 1 ÷ f**: the period is one divided by the frequency.
And it all links up in the **wave equation**: **speed = frequency × wavelength**.
So if a speaker sends out **340** waves a second, and sound covers **340 metres** in that second, each wave must be **1 metre** long.
In air, sound has the same speed whatever its pitch. So a **higher frequency** must mean a **shorter wavelength**.
Waves come in two families, sorted by the direction of the **vibration** compared with the direction the wave travels.
In a **longitudinal** wave, the vibrations go **back and forth, along** the direction of travel, making compressions and rarefactions.
Push a slinky spring in and out, and squashes and stretches travel along it. **Sound is longitudinal**.
In a **transverse** wave, the vibrations are **at right angles** to the direction of travel.
Flick a rope up and down: the wobble travels along, but each bit of rope just moves up and down, making **crests** and **troughs**.
**Light** is transverse, like all electromagnetic waves. So are the **ripples** on water.
Both kinds carry **energy** without carrying the material along. The difference is the direction of vibration: **along** the wave, or **across** it.
At the other end from ultrasound is **infrasound**: sound **below 20 Hz**, too **low** for us to hear.
**Elephants** use deep infrasound rumbles to keep in touch with herds kilometres away, and can even sense them through their feet.
**Whales** make very low calls that carry across huge distances of ocean.
**Earthquakes**, **volcanoes** and big **storms** make infrasound too, and scientists use special detectors to pick it up and help give warnings.
Some animals seem to sense it before people notice anything, which may be why they act strangely before an earthquake.
So between infrasound below **20 Hz** and ultrasound above **20,000 Hz**, the sound we hear is just a **slice** of it all.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Fast Pitch, Big Bang**: frequency sets the pitch; amplitude sets the loudness.
**No air, no aware**: no medium, no sound.
**Solids Speed, Gases Go slow.**
**20 to 20k**: our hearing range, in hertz.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: sound **can't** travel through a vacuum. There are no particles to vibrate.
Two: **pitch** depends on **frequency**, and **loudness** depends on **amplitude**. Don't mix them up.
Three: the particles **don't travel** with the wave. They vibrate; it's the **energy** that travels.
Four: sound is about **340 m/s**, and light about **300,000,000 m/s**. They're not similar at all!
Five: in echo and sonar sums, the sound goes **there and back**, so cut the distance **in half**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
Why can't sound travel through a vacuum?
A vacuum has **no particles** to pass the vibration along.
A sound gets louder, but its pitch stays the same. What has changed?
Its **amplitude** is bigger. Its frequency is the same.
Is sound fastest through air, water or steel?
**Steel.** Sound is fastest in solids.
What is ultrasound?
Sound **above 20,000 Hz**: too high for humans to hear.
You see lightning, then hear the thunder 3 seconds later. About how far away is the storm?
About **1 kilometre**: three seconds, divided by three.
Brilliant work. Now try the Sound quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
